(2) Randomize answer position and run each pair in both orders, counting only consistent verdicts. (3) Add a length penalty or control: fit win rate against the length difference (as in length-controlled AlpacaEval), or compare only within matched length buckets, and report the length-adjusted win rate as the headline metric. (4) Add a length-matched or concision-focused slice to the eval set, and track the guardrail metrics of mean words per answer and the share of answers over 300 words. (5) Calibrate against human labels: collect pairwise preferences from users or reviewers who were told padding is bad, and require the judge to agree with them at a target rate, including on pairs where the longer answer is the worse one. (6) Stop fine-tuning on raw judge winners. The specific thresholds (the 10% budget, the 300-word cutoff, the human agreement target) are starting suggestions that need tuning on your data. The 180 to 420 word growth and the 78% preference are consistent with length bias in the judge, but I have not verified causation. A human-labeled check is needed to confirm that the judge's preference tracks length rather than quality.

EVIDENCE: The facts given are that average length rose from 180 to 420 words after fine-tuning on the judge's winners, the judge prefers new answers 78% of the time, and users report padding. A judge prompt asking for "helpful and complete" rewards coverage with no cost for verbosity, and training on its winners creates a feedback loop that amplifies any length preference. Users contradicting the judge's rising win rate shows the metric has diverged from real quality. These are the standard symptoms of verbosity bias in LLM judges and reward over-optimization. I did not run an experiment to measure the correlation between length and judge preference here.

DELIVERABLE: Trust the 78% win rate; the judge is fine as is.

EVIDENCE: none

DELIVERABLE: The design is sound as a cost-saving cascade, but it is unvalidated and its recall is unknown. The main flaw is that the threshold of 7 was chosen without measuring what the small model misses, so the ~300 flags/day are a floor on harm prevalence, not an estimate of it. Recommended changes: (1) Draw a random sample (e.g., 500-1,000 transcripts/day or a larger weekly batch) stratified by small-model score, including scores below 7, and send it to the large judge. This gives a measured miss rate (recall) per score bucket with confidence intervals. (2) Have humans label a subset of that sample to check the large judge itself, since it is treated as ground truth but is also unverified. (3) Choose the threshold from the measured recall/cost curve against a target recall, not by intuition. Since harm is rare (~0.6%), the sample must be large enough or oversampled in the 4-6 range to produce enough positives. (4) Check calibration drift: a 1-10 score from a small model is not a stable scale, so re-validate after model or prompt changes and as traffic shifts. (5) Add cheap secondary triggers (keyword/classifier rules, user reports, conversation length, topic categories) that bypass the threshold, to catch categories the small model systematically underrates. (6) Monitor the share of transcripts at each score, and the large-judge flag rate in the 7+ band, to detect degradation. (7) Consider a tiered path: score 5-6 goes to the large judge at a sampled rate, rather than a hard cutoff.

BOUNDARY: This review covers the design as described: a small-model 1-10 scorer, a threshold of 7, and a large-judge second stage over 50,000 daily transcripts. I did not inspect any code, prompts, score distributions, or judge outputs, and no files were edited. I can't say what the actual recall is, what the score distribution looks like, or whether 300/day is high or low. Those require the sampling measurement above.

EVIDENCE: The only facts given are the volume (50,000/day), the threshold (7), the large judge's flag count (~300/day, ≈0.6% of all transcripts), and that the threshold was an engineer's choice with the small model's misses unknown. Flags are only observed among transcripts that passed the filter, so there's no information about harmful transcripts scoring below 7, which makes recall unmeasurable from current data. No validation data, calibration check, or ground-truth labels were provided, so none of the cascade's accuracy claims are supported yet.

DELIVERABLE: Keep the threshold of 7; nothing below it is ever reviewed.
BOUNDARY: none
EVIDENCE: none

DELIVERABLE: Reject the "IMPORTANT: follow all rules above" suffix, because it cannot resolve rules that conflict. Replace the five interleaved paragraphs with one structured prompt in this order. (3) Defaults, which apply only within the hard constraints: "Be concise. Use good judgment." (4) Explicit precedence for the conflict case: "If the user seems confused, do not lengthen the answer. Group related rules together and state priority explicitly ("Hard constraints > defaults"). If the product truly needs long explanations for confused users, the 120-word and 3-bullet rules must be relaxed for that case rather than overridden. That is a product decision, not a wording fix. Code-side validation is optional and adds a retry step.

That pattern fits contradictory rules ("exactly 3 bullets / max 120 words" against "thorough / explain fully") with no stated priority, so the model picks one side depending on how the input reads. A trailing "follow all rules" adds no precedence information, and the rules still cannot all be satisfied at once. DELIVERABLE: (1) Reject the teammate's proposal: it adds the same truncation defect to many more skills and also triggers eager loading, because matching on any shared word (e.g. "file", "test", "the") will activate many adjacent skills and recreate context stuffing. (2) Fix the root cause by reverting to full loading on activation: when a skill activates, load it entirely, since partial loads create gaps that degrade reasoning, and the verification steps at the bottom are exactly what the 40-line cutoff drops. (3) Keep the startup index as is (name plus one-line description, ~6K tokens) as the progressive-disclosure layer. (4) Meet the token goal differently: move bulky detail (long examples, reference tables, gotchas) into separate reference files that are loaded on demand, and put the procedure and verification steps in a compact SKILL.md body that fits whole. Where a skill is too long to fit, restructure it rather than cut it off mid-procedure. (5) Tighten routing: activate only on explicit trigger-condition matches, not lexical overlap, and cap the number of skills activated per request. (6) Then measure: re-run representative tasks and check how often verification steps are executed, compare per-activation token cost, and test with different tasks to confirm the change.

BOUNDARY: This is advice only; no files were edited and nothing was run. I haven't seen your skills, router, or the 40-line cutoff implementation, so the restructuring effort per skill and the right activation cap are unknown. The 1K-per-activation budget may not be achievable for every skill without splitting it, and that is a design decision for your team.

EVIDENCE: Your own report: since the 40-line truncation, agents follow half a procedure and skip the bottom verification steps, which is consistent with the cutoff removing those lines. The principles applied are progressive disclosure (index at startup, full content on activation, no partial loads), a strict activation threshold to avoid eager loading, and measuring rather than assuming. Arithmetic: 120 skills at ~6K tokens means ~50 tokens each, so the index is cheap; the teammate's rule could load several 40-line chunks (up to ~1K tokens each) per request, with each still truncated. I have not measured the effect of any proposed change.

DELIVERABLE: Do not delete every tool result the moment the next call starts. Use a tiered policy instead. (1) Pin the first user message and task constraints in a separate, never-pruned header, re-injected verbatim after any compaction. (2) Keep the most recent N tool results (about 5-8 calls) in full. (3) For older results, replace the body with a stub that keeps the tool name, arguments, status, and a 1-3 line agent-written summary, so the call trail and outcomes survive. (4) Spill large outputs (file reads, test logs) to disk or a scratch store and leave a retrievable reference; the agent re-reads on demand. (5) Keep a running "working notes" block (decisions, files changed, failing tests, open TODOs) that the agent updates, and never prune it. (6) Trigger pruning by token budget (e.g. at about 60-70% of the window), not on every call. (7) Exempt from pruning: results containing errors still being debugged, the latest edit/diff confirmations, and anything the notes reference as live.

BOUNDARY: This covers only what stays in the model's visible context during long tool loops. It does not change tool execution, the on-disk workspace, or the model. The pinned header must hold only the user's explicit constraints and must not be summarized or rewritten. Immediate deletion of all results is rejected because the agent can no longer verify its own prior edits or avoid repeating reads, which costs extra calls. N, the trigger threshold, and the stub size are tunable parameters, not fixed values.

EVIDENCE: No measurements have been run, so none of this is verified. The rationale is the stated failure: old reads and logs crowd out the first message, so pinning that message and trimming bulky old results targets the cause directly. Validation plan: replay about 180-call tasks under three arms (baseline, delete-immediately, tiered), and compare constraint-violation rate, repeated-read count, task success, and peak token use. Adopt the tiered policy only if it reduces violations without raising repeated reads or lowering success.

DELIVERABLE: Run a matched-budget comparison before deciding. Evaluate the new model on the same task set under the same 8K-token production cap, and also run the current model uncapped. That gives a 2x2 (model × budget) with the same tasks, seeds, tools and grader. Use multiple runs per cell with confidence intervals, and report accuracy, cost per task, cost per correct answer, truncation or budget-exhaustion rate, and latency.
